cls: Passive immunising agent - heterologous (equine) anti-rabies immunoglobulin
pharm: Purified equine immunoglobulin providing immediate, passive rabies-virus-neutralising antibody at the wound and systemically during rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, bridging the gap until active vaccine immunity develops
quick: 40 IU/kg body weight once, infiltrated around the wound(s) with any remainder given IM
Not a contraindication; rabies PEP is given regardless of pregnancy (rabies is fatal)
Not a contraindication; give as part of indicated PEP
Anaphylaxis/immediate reactions; later serum sickness; wound infiltration completeness
summary: Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) is a purified heterologous (horse-derived) anti-rabies immunoglobulin used for passive immunisation as part of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in category III (and category II in immunocompromised) exposures. It provides immediate rabies-virus-neutralising antibody to cover the period before the rabies vaccine induces active immunity. The WHO-recommended dose is 40 IU/kg body weight (versus 20 IU/kg for human rabies immunoglobulin), given as a single administration with as much as anatomically feasible infiltrated into and around all bite wounds and any remainder injected intramuscularly. It must always be combined with a full course of rabies vaccine (given at a different site) and thorough wound washing. ERIG can cause hypersensitivity reactions, including rare anaphylaxis and delayed serum sickness; modern highly purified F(ab')2 products have a lower reaction rate and routine prior skin testing is no longer recommended by WHO. This product is not in openFDA; dosing follows WHO and national rabies guidelines.
indications: Passive immunisation in rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for category III exposures (transdermal bites/scratches, contamination of mucous membrane with saliva, bat exposures)
Category II exposures in immunocompromised persons
Always combined with rabies vaccine and wound care in previously unvaccinated individuals

moa: Equine rabies immunoglobulin supplies preformed, exogenous rabies-virus-neutralising antibodies that bind and neutralise rabies virus at the inoculation site and in the circulation, providing immediate passive protection. Because the rabies vaccine takes about 7-14 days to generate protective active antibody, infiltrating immunoglobulin around the wound neutralises virus locally during this vulnerable window, reducing the chance of the virus reaching the nervous system. The passive antibody is gradually catabolised as active vaccine-induced immunity takes over.

absolute: There is essentially no absolute contraindication when given for a genuine category III rabies exposure, because untreated rabies is almost universally fatal
relative: Known severe hypersensitivity to equine serum/immunoglobulin (use human rabies immunoglobulin if available)
Previously fully vaccinated persons (immunoglobulin not needed)
Presentation more than 7 days after starting the vaccine series
monitor: Immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis during and shortly after administration
Delayed serum sickness (fever, rash, arthralgia) over the following 1-2 weeks
Concurrent vaccine administration at a separate site

preg: Rabies is almost invariably fatal, so pregnancy is NOT a contraindication to post-exposure prophylaxis; equine rabies immunoglobulin should be given as indicated together with rabies vaccine. The benefit of preventing rabies far outweighs any theoretical risk.
lact: Breastfeeding is not a contraindication. Equine rabies immunoglobulin should be administered as part of indicated post-exposure prophylaxis; breastfeeding can continue.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment; the immunoglobulin is cleared by physiological protein catabolism rather than renal excretion.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: Excess immunoglobulin dose - exceeding 40 IU/kg can partially suppress the active antibody response to rabies vaccine; do not exceed the recommended dose
moderate: Live vaccines - passively administered antibody may interfere with the response to some live vaccines given around the same time (rabies vaccine itself is not live and is unaffected)
interactions.diagnostics: Passively acquired antibodies may transiently affect serologic test interpretation

common: Local pain, redness or swelling at the injection/infiltration site
serious: Serum sickness (fever, urticaria, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy) typically 1-2 weeks later
emergency: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise, hypotension or shock

monitoring: Observe for immediate hypersensitivity reactions during and after administration
Watch for delayed serum sickness over the following 1-2 weeks
Confirm thorough wound washing and complete wound infiltration
Ensure the full rabies vaccine course is given and completed
Have adrenaline and resuscitation equipment immediately available
counsel: This injection gives instant protection while the rabies vaccine builds your own immunity - you must complete the full vaccine course as well
Most of the dose is injected around the bite wound(s); some may go into a muscle
Tell staff immediately if you feel faint, develop a widespread rash, swelling of the face/throat or difficulty breathing
In the next 1-2 weeks watch for fever, joint pains or a rash (serum sickness) and report them
Keep all follow-up vaccine appointments - rabies is preventable but otherwise almost always fatal
pk: Local neutralising antibody available immediately; systemic peak within a few days
Equine F(ab')2/immunoglobulin half-life roughly 2-7 days (shorter than human immunoglobulin's ~21 days)
Provides cover for about 1-2 weeks until vaccine-induced active immunity develops
Store at 2-8 C; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Dose is 40 IU/kg (equine) versus 20 IU/kg for human rabies immunoglobulin - do not exceed it (excess suppresses vaccine response)
Infiltrate as much as feasible into/around ALL wounds; give remainder IM at a site away from the vaccine
Must always accompany a full rabies vaccine course plus thorough wound washing - never used alone
Modern purified F(ab')2 products have low reaction rates; WHO no longer recommends routine prior skin testing
Not found in openFDA (biological/heterologous serum); dosing follows WHO and national rabies guidelines
missed: Not applicable - equine rabies immunoglobulin is a single, supervised administration during post-exposure prophylaxis, not a repeated self-administered medicine. If it could not be given on day 0, it may still be given up to day 7 of the vaccine series.
overdose: Giving more than 40 IU/kg does not increase protection and may partially suppress the active immune response to the rabies vaccine; the calculated dose should not be exceeded. Acute overdose is otherwise managed supportively, watching for hypersensitivity and volume-related effects.
